points.source_note: CORRECTED 2026-09-10 (re-verified via WebFetch): the source's own text says the 0.3 Wh figure assumes H100 GPUs at 'server-level power consumption of ~1500 W per GPU due to the overhead costs of servers and data centers, reflecting full data-center scope rather than GPU-only' -- so this is a full_stack measurement, not active_accelerator as originally recorded (which had wrongly applied the 2.4x FullStackFactor on top of an already-full-stack figure). Epoch AI's GPT-4o estimate: ~0.3 Wh for a ~500-output-token typical query ('roughly a full page of typed text'), described by the authors as 'relatively pessimistic', about 1/10th the older 3 Wh figure. The article does not quote GPT-4o API pricing directly; price used as the output-price proxy is OpenAI's GPT-4o API list price at the time ($2.50 in / $10.00 out per MTok, matching the gpt-4o-2024-08-06 pricing current as of 2025-01).

Re-verified 2026-09-10 via WebFetch (arxiv.org/html/2508.15734, Table 1): 'the median Gemini Apps text prompt consumes 0.24 Wh of energy' (comprehensive/full-stack approach) versus 0.10 Wh/prompt for the 'existing approach' (active AI accelerators only); the 0.24 Wh breaks down as 0.10 Wh accelerator + 0.06 Wh CPU & DRAM + 0.02 Wh idle machines + 0.02 Wh overhead. Both figures confirmed exactly as originally recorded; the 2.4x ratio (0.24/0.10) is FullStackFactor's source. The paper does not publish a token count for the median prompt; 500 output tokens is this implementation's documented assumption, hence the low weight. Price proxy is Gemini 2.5 Flash list pricing, the closest current-catalog model to the assistant tier the median prompt describes.

Attempted re-verification 2026-09-10: both the primary URL (cell.com) and its ScienceDirect mirror (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435126001145) returned HTTP 403 (paywalled); could not fetch full text. The headline figures this row is built from (0.31 Wh median, IQR 0.16-0.60, across the paper's frontier model set) are independently corroborated by third-party summaries of the paper's abstract/press coverage found via web search, which is the best available confirmation without journal access. Left as originally recorded: this row uses the geometric mean of the paper's reported 0.0001-0.002 Wh/output-token range (sqrt(1e-4 * 2e-3) = 4.47e-4 Wh/token = 447 Wh/MTok) directly rather than assuming an output-token count for the 0.31 Wh median, and is left vendor-unassigned (contributes only to the pooled fit) since it spans multiple vendors' models. Flagging for a follow-up re-check if journal access becomes available.

Re-verified 2026-09-10 via WebFetch: gist (dated March 9, 2026, citing Claude Code sessions Jan 2026 / Simon P. Couch's analysis and Faros AI / Restato token-economy breakdowns) confirms the four figures exactly -- output ~1,950 Wh/MTok, input ~390 Wh/MTok, cache creation ~490 Wh/MTok, cache read ~39 Wh/MTok (ratio 1 : 5 : 1.25 : 0.1 against input, i.e. built directly from Anthropic's own list-price ratios at $15/MTok out). No changes. This is the estimator's primary anchor, hence the highest weight.

Re-verified 2026-09-10 via WebFetch: METHODOLOGY.md confirms 1.0 J/token base compute energy times a PUE of 1.2 (1.0 * 1.2 / 3600 = 333.33 Wh/MTok) for Claude Sonnet, documented as a deliberately conservative lower bound (no serving overhead beyond PUE) with 'Low confidence' on the derived tiers. Haiku (0.3 J/token) and Opus (2.0 J/token) are inferred from Sonnet's price ratio (~3:1 to Haiku, ~2:1 to Opus), the same technique this estimator uses. No changes.

CORRECTED 2026-09-10 (re-verified via WebFetch, Table 4): the short-prompt bucket is explicitly '100 input-300 output' tokens, not the unitemized 300-output-only assumption originally recorded (tokens_in was 0). Claude-3.7 Sonnet: 0.836 +/- 0.102 Wh/query on a 10.20 kW critical-power H100/H200 node at batch size 8. Small fixed-batch node measurements are kept for cross-model SHAPE only, hence the low weight.

CORRECTED 2026-09-10 (re-verified via WebFetch, Table 4): the medium-prompt bucket is explicitly '1k input-1k output' tokens -- both the output count (was wrongly 800, not the paper's 1000) and the input count (was 0, ignoring the input tokens entirely) were wrong in the original row; this is the largest correction of the re-verification pass, since ignoring 1000 input tokens materially understated the output-equivalent-token denominator. Claude-3.7 Sonnet: 2.781 +/- 0.277 Wh/query, same 10.20 kW/batch-8 node. Shape-only, low weight.

CORRECTED 2026-09-10 (re-verified via WebFetch, Table 4): the long-prompt bucket is explicitly '10k input-1.5k output' tokens; tokens_out=1500 was already correct but tokens_in was wrongly 0, ignoring 10,000 input tokens entirely -- the biggest input-to-output ratio of the three buckets, so this was the most-understated row before the fix. Claude-3.7 Sonnet: 5.518 +/- 0.751 Wh/query, same 10.20 kW/batch-8 node. Confirmed the paper benchmarks 30 models including GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-4.1 nano, o3, o4-mini, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1; only the Claude 3.7 Sonnet figures were available to this implementation, so the other models are not yet represented as points here. Shape-only, low weight.

COULD NOT CONFIRM 2026-09-10: fetched both the HTML and PDF full text (via WebFetch and a local pypdf text extraction of the PDF, since the HTML fetch could not read Figures 2/4's numeric axis labels -- they are embedded as unmapped custom-font glyphs, not extractable text). The literal string '0.39' does not appear anywhere in the extracted text, and the paper's only explicit FP8-vs-FP16 quantization case study (Figure 6) is for Llama 3 405B, not the 70B model this row cites; the paper's per-model absolute-Wh/J batch-size sweep (Figure 4) explicitly covers batch sizes 32-1024 only, not batch-1/unbatched, even though batch 1 is named elsewhere as one of the methodology's swept parameters in the abstract. I cannot verify this row's specific 'LLaMA3-70B, FP8, unbatched, 0.39 J/token' figure against the source and cannot rule out misattribution; the unit conversion (0.39 J/token / 3600 = 108.33 Wh/MTok) is arithmetically correct if the input figure is right, but the input figure itself is unconfirmed. Weight cut from 0.3 to 0.08 to reflect this; kept rather than deleted since removing it outright would need a documented replacement, and no better LLaMA3-70B figure was found in the paper's extractable text either. Recommend a follow-up with a properly OCR'd copy of the paper (or contacting the authors) before trusting this row's absolute level; its influence on the pooled fit is now small given the reduced weight. Price proxy (approximate OpenRouter list rate for Llama-3-70B-Instruct, since Meta does not sell API access directly) is unaffected by this doubt and unchanged.

PARTIALLY CONFIRMED 2026-09-10: the cited ai-energy-score-v2 roundup post does not itself contain a specific gpt-oss-120b number (it only discusses GPT-OSS in passing re: reasoning-mode energy). The '8.5 kWh per 1,000 queries' figure (= 8.5 Wh/query) is independently corroborated via web search summarizing the AI Energy Score Leaderboard (huggingface.co/spaces/AIEnergyScore/Leaderboard, a JS-rendered Space WebFetch could not load directly). The same author's companion deep-dive post (huggingface.co/blog/sasha/gpt-oss-energy, Aug 7 2025) measured gpt-oss-120b directly at 1.84 / 3.83 / 8.31 Wh for 25/50/100 output tokens on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs (batch size 1, 100 prompts from the 'Awesome ChatGPT Prompts' dataset) -- NOT H100 as this row previously claimed; corrected that claim to 'GPU model unconfirmed for the Leaderboard figure' since the Leaderboard's own hardware was not directly verifiable. 8.31 Wh at 100 output tokens is close in order of magnitude to the row's 8.5 Wh/query, supporting the row's validity even though the exact 200-output-token assumption for the Leaderboard figure specifically remains this implementation's own assumption, not confirmed in either source. Unbatched single-GPU serving is far less efficient than production batched serving, hence the low weight -- the resulting Wh/MTok is expected to look high.
